paragraphs.heading: What ocean temperature means
paragraphs.text: The term ocean temperature covers how warm the sea is at any depth. It can also be used more narrowly, for water that is not near the surface, and then it means the same thing as deep ocean temperature. Experts take temperatures at different depths and use them to calculate a figure called ocean heat content.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Temperature plays a crucial part in the global climate system, in ocean currents and in the habitats of sea life. Together with dissolved oxygen, it has a big influence on many aspects of the ocean. These two affect the ocean's primary productivity, its carbon cycle, its nutrient cycles and its ecosystems. They act alongside salinity and density to control whether water mixes or stays in layers, and to control ocean currents.

paragraphs.heading: From the surface to the deep
paragraphs.text: Ocean temperature changes with depth, with place and with season. It also depends on how much solar radiation falls on the surface. In the tropics, where the Sun is nearly overhead, the surface layers can climb above 30 °C. Near the poles, water in equilibrium with sea ice sits at about −2 °C. Deep ocean water is cold and salty, with a very uniform temperature of around 0-3 °C, and it accounts for about 90% of all ocean water by volume.

paragraphs.heading: Water on the move
paragraphs.text: Water circulates through the oceans continuously and on a large scale. One part of this is the thermohaline circulation, which is driven by global differences in density that surface heat and freshwater flows create. Warm surface currents cool as they travel away from the tropics, and the water grows denser and sinks. Changes in temperature and density then carry the cold water back toward the equator as a deep current. In time it wells up toward the surface again.

paragraphs.heading: Taking the sea's temperature
paragraphs.text: There are various ways to measure ocean temperature. The basic one is to lower a device that records temperature and other things electronically. It is called a CTD, short for conductivity, temperature and depth, and it sends its data up to the ship all the time through a conducting cable. Below the surface it is important to state the exact depth of a reading, since temperature varies a lot with depth. This is especially true by day, when low wind and a lot of sunshine may form a warm layer at the top with big changes in temperature further down. Experts call these strong daytime changes of temperature with depth a diurnal thermocline.

paragraphs.heading: A warming ocean
paragraphs.text: Climate change is warming the oceans, and the rate of warming is increasing. The fastest warming is in the upper ocean, above 700 m, but the trend reaches throughout the ocean. In 2022 the global ocean was the hottest that humans have ever recorded. The rise in temperature, both at the surface and deeper down, is an important effect of climate change on the oceans.
